issues.legal_issue: A religion-specific restriction on charitable and religious testamentary bequests is invalid when its classifications and conditions lack a reasonable connection to its stated purpose.
material_facts: A law restricted charitable or religious bequests by Christian testators who had a nephew, niece, or nearer relative unless the will was made sufficiently long before death, deposited within a specified period, and kept in deposit until death.
Testators belonging to other religious communities were not subject to the same restriction.

The restriction could defeat a bequest because the testator died within the required period or did not meet the deposit conditions, circumstances unrelated to the charitable purpose of the bequest and not necessarily within the testator’s control.

The stated purpose was to prevent ill-considered deathbed bequests made under religious influence; the Court noted that safeguards against wills made through fraud, coercion, or loss of free agency already existed.
The restriction treated religious and charitable bequests alike, although the Court found no justification for limiting charitable bequests on the stated ground.
issues.conclusion: The restriction was unreasonable, arbitrary, and discriminatory, and therefore violated the constitutional guarantee of equality.
issues.legal_principle: The equality guarantee permits a classification only if it rests on an intelligible differentia and that differentia has a rational nexus to the object sought to be achieved. The Court applied Article 14 and considered the protection against fraud, coercion, and loss of free agency under Section 51 of the Indian Succession Act, 1925, as well as the general testamentary capacity and execution provisions in Sections 59 and 63. It also relied on DLF Qutab Enclave Complex Educational Charitable Trust v. State of Haryana and Kapila Hingorani v. State of Bihar for strict construction of restrictions on property rights and for considering changes over time when assessing constitutionality; the concurring opinion also referred to D.S. Nakara v. Union of India on reasonable classification.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_testamentary: The proceeding challenges the constitutionality of a rule restricting testamentary bequests.
predicates.restriction_applies_to_one_religious_com: The rule imposes the restriction on testators belonging to one religious community.
predicates.comparable_bequests_by_other_communities: Testators in other religious communities may make comparable bequests without the same restriction.
predicates.charitable_bequest_depends_on_testator_s: A charitable bequest can fail because the testator does not live for a specified period after making the will.
predicates.charitable_bequest_depends_on_will_depos: A charitable bequest can fail because the testator does not satisfy conditions for depositing and keeping the will in deposit.
predicates.survival_and_deposit_conditions_do_not_a: The testator’s survival for a specified period and compliance with deposit conditions do not further the stated aim of preventing bequests made under improper influence.

issues.definition: When a constitutional challenge concerns a testamentary restriction applied to one religious community, comparable bequests by others are unrestricted, and the restriction’s survival and deposit conditions do not advance its stated purpose, the restriction is unconstitutional.

issues.legal_issue: A restriction on testamentary rights that affects a class associated with a religion does not, for that reason alone, constitute discrimination against an individual on the ground of religion under the constitutional guarantee against such discrimination.
material_facts: The challenged restriction limited the testamentary rights of Christian testators in specified circumstances.
The petitioners relied on the fact that the restriction applied to Christians and not to other religious communities.
issues.conclusion: The constitutional guarantee against discrimination on grounds including religion did not apply to the challenge in this case.
issues.legal_principle: Article 15(1) prohibits discrimination against a citizen on specified grounds, including religion, and the right it confers is an individual right concerning the citizen’s rights, privileges, and immunities. The Court distinguished an individual claim of discrimination on a prohibited ground from a law that restricts the testamentary rights of a class of citizens associated with a religion.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_testamentary: The proceeding challenges a restriction on testamentary rights as unconstitutional.
predicates.restriction_limits_rights_of_a_religious: The restriction applies to a class of citizens identified by their religious community.
predicates.claim_is_only_that_the_class_is_religiou: The discrimination claim rests on the fact that the affected class is religiously defined.

issues.definition: When a constitutional challenge concerns a testamentary restriction on a religiously defined class and the claim rests only on that classification, the classification alone does not establish individual discrimination on grounds of religion.

issues.legal_issue: A limitation on testamentary gifts for religious or charitable purposes does not infringe constitutional religious-freedom guarantees where making such gifts has not been established as an essential part of religious practice.
material_facts: The restriction concerned the disposition of property by will for religious or charitable purposes.
The petitioners asserted that charitable and religious giving was part of Christian faith, but did not establish that making such a disposition was compulsory or an integral part of that faith.
The Court treated succession and testamentary disposition as matters of a secular character and noted that a person could remain Christian without making a charitable or religious bequest.
issues.conclusion: The restriction did not violate the constitutional guarantees of religious freedom or the right of religious denominations to manage their affairs.
issues.legal_principle: Article 25 protects freedom of conscience and the profession and practice of religion, including its integral religious practices; a recommended or pious act is not, without more, an integral part of a religion. The Court referred to Stainislaus Rev. v. State of M.P. on the meaning of profession and practice, and to Sarla Mudgal, President, Kalyani v. Union of India for the principle that succession and similar secular matters are not within the guarantees in Articles 25 and 26. The Court held that Article 26 did not apply for the same reasons.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_alleging_interf: The proceeding alleges that a limit on testamentary giving interferes with religious freedom.
predicates.rule_regulates_secular_property_disposit: The rule concerns how a person may dispose of property by will.
predicates.religious_bequest_not_established_as_ess: The claimants do not establish that making a religious or charitable bequest is an essential practice of their religion.

issues.definition: When a religious-freedom challenge concerns a rule about secular testamentary disposition and the bequest is not established as an essential religious practice, the rule does not violate the religious-freedom guarantees.

issues.legal_issue: A law enacted before the Constitution remains subject to review for inconsistency with fundamental rights and is not validated merely by its continued operation after the Constitution came into force.
material_facts: The challenged testamentary restriction was part of legislation enacted before the Constitution.
The legislation continued to operate after the Constitution came into force.
issues.conclusion: The law’s pre-constitutional enactment and continued operation did not prevent review of its consistency with fundamental rights.
issues.legal_principle: Article 13(1) makes pre-constitutional laws void to the extent that they are inconsistent with fundamental rights, while Article 372 continues existing laws subject to the Constitution. The Court relied on Keshavan Madhava Menon v. The State of Bombay and explained that an inconsistent provision is void prospectively from the commencement of the Constitution.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_preconstitut: The proceeding challenges the consistency of a law enacted before the Constitution with fundamental rights.
predicates.law_remained_in_force_after_constitution: The law continued to operate after the Constitution came into force.

issues.definition: When a constitutional challenge concerns a pre-constitutional law that remained in force after the Constitution came into force, the law remains subject to review for consistency with fundamental rights.
